Triggers.value: People who look similar to the victims

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I detach myself from the memories

Threat.value: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper
The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
issues.explanation: The inaction/self-blame item is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of childhood physical abuse by a caregiver. In a child victim context, 'not doing more to stop what happened' implies agency that is typically not clinically plausible for the same trauma profile; a more general shame/self-blame item would fit, but this specific omission-guilt wording is questionable.

Within the Threat node, 'difficulty concentrating' is not a threat appraisal but a general arousal/cognitive symptom. The other Threat items reflect current danger and hypervigilance ('strong physical reactions to reminders', 'need to stay alert to fall asleep'). This item weakens within-node coherence and does not match the node's formulation role as perceived current threat.

vignette:
Tane was born on a small Pacific island, the eldest of five children in a household where his father's love was measured in silence and his punishments in open-handed blows. The beatings began before he could remember a time without them-a belt across the thighs, a fist to the ribs, the sting of a wooden spoon broken on his back. There was no pattern: sometimes a bad grade, sometimes a spilled drink, sometimes nothing at all. What Tane learned was that safety was an illusion and that his own body was a site of shame. He learned to stay small. By the time he left home at seventeen, he had buried the memories under a quiet, watchful competence that later made him an excellent detective.

But the past never stays buried. Now fifty-six, divorced, living alone in a cramped apartment near the precinct, Tane is a walking archive of unwelcome returns. A case came in three months ago-a domestic that ended with a fire. When he stepped onto the scene, the acrid smell of burnt insulation and melted plastic hit his nostrils, and suddenly he was ten years old, pinned against the kitchen wall, the smell of his father's cigarette mixing with the scorch of a hot iron. The trigger brought the full memory without warning: the rage, the helplessness, the burning shame. He stood frozen in the hallway, his heart hammering, while his partner called his name. That night, he could not sleep because he needed to stay alert-to what, he could not name. Already running on that background hum of danger, he found that almost anything could tip into a warning-a car backfiring, a raised voice, the smell of cigarette smoke drifting from a neighbor's window. Every creak of the floorboards was a threat. Because the memory had surfaced so vividly, he began to see warnings everywhere: in a distant siren, in the clatter of a dropped key, in the way a stranger's footsteps slowed outside his door.

Since then, Tane has become a master of avoidance. He avoids wearing any dark-colored shirts that might resemble the ones his father favored. He avoids people as much as possible, staying late at the station to dodge the crowds at happy hour. When a witness-a middle-aged man with a broad face and tired eyes-walked into the interrogation room, Tane felt his jaw tighten. The man looked nothing like his father, yet the resemblance in posture, in the way he sat, triggered something. Tane cut the interview short. He has also grown expert at detaching himself from the memories: when a flashback surfaces, he mentally steps sideways, blanking his mind, pushing the images away into a grey fog. But the detachment never lasts. Lying in bed, he feels the rage on recall-a hot, helpless fury that makes his fists clench and his breathing turn ragged. He has come to believe that his reactions since the event prove he is a lousy coper. A real detective would be able to handle a smell, a face. The event happened to him because of the sort of person he is, he tells himself: weak, defective, deserving. This belief that he was defective kept dragging him back into the memory of that night, as if his mind needed to confirm the verdict.

His shattered beliefs about the world are reinforced every time a memory intrudes. He used to think the world made sense, that people got what they deserved. Now he sees only randomness and cruelty. When he tries to explain what happened to his therapist-a middle-aged woman who asked about his childhood three sessions ago-he loses the thread and cannot finish. The words collapse. The rage rises, and he clams up. His therapist says he is doing well, but Tane knows that avoidance only makes it worse. The more he detaches, the more the memories burst through without warning. The more he avoids people, the more hypervigilant he becomes, scanning every face for potential danger. His physical reactivity-the pounding heart, the sweaty palms-convinces him that he is broken. Last week, during a surveillance operation, he saw a man in a blue jacket standing near a car, and his body reacted before his mind caught up: he ducked behind a dumpster, breath coming in short gasps. It was just a man waiting for a ride. But Tane's threat system had already hijacked him, and afterward he berated himself for being a coward.

Positive emotions confuse him most of all. At his daughter's wedding two years ago, he felt a swell of happiness watching her dance. Then a wave of panic hit him. Joy felt dangerous, like a trap. He left early, blaming a migraine. Now he finds himself suspicious of laughter, of any warmth. The causal loops have tightened into a noose: a trigger brings the memory; the memory ratchets up threat; threat feeds his negative appraisals; those appraisals make him avoid; avoidance makes triggers more potent. He is exhausted.

What finally brought Tane to the veterans' mental health clinic-though he never served in the military, only in the police force-was an ultimatum from his captain after he froze during a routine evidence search in a burnt-out apartment building. He sat in the waiting room with his hands on his knees, certain he would fail at this too. What he fears most is that his mind is permanent: that the man who beat him has won, that all these years of being a detective were just a long delay before the collapse. What he hopes for, barely daring to whisper it even to himself, is that someone might show him how to put the memories away for good.

violations.explanation: Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette does not show that negative appraisals cause intrusive memories; instead, memories reinforce negative appraisals.
Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not demonstrate that the memory itself leads to increased triggering; it shows triggers leading to memory.
Threat → Triggers: There is no direct causal link where a sense of threat makes triggers more potent or more frequent; avoidance is shown to mediate that effect.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette does not show that negative appraisals cause intrusive memories; instead, memories reinforce negative appraisals.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Memory → Triggers: Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not demonstrate that the memory itself leads to increased triggering; it shows triggers leading to memory.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Triggers: Threat → Triggers: There is no direct causal link where a sense of threat makes triggers more potent or more frequent; avoidance is shown to mediate that effect.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
